extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in patent analytics, NLP, and information retrieval (including patent examiners and ML engineers)
extracted.subtask_description: Survey of patent analysis tasks, evaluation measures, and methodologies (classification, retrieval, information extraction, novelty/inventiveness prediction, FTO, landscaping, etc.) intended to guide research and benchmarking in patent NLP/IR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent analysis task taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent analysis tasks are divided into four main types: subject classification, information retrieval, quality assessment, and technology insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type comprises sub-tasks (e.g., subject classification; retrieval splits into patent retrieval and information extraction; quality assessment includes novelty prediction, granting prediction, litigation prediction, and patent valuation; technology insights include forecasting and innovation recommendation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated subject classification (task definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi-label classification task where the aim is to predict patents' specific categories or classes based on patent content (title, abstract, claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents may belong to multiple classes; classification assists database organization and examiner workflows. Input is a sequence of tokens x=[w1,...,wn], output label y in {y1,...,ym}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hierarchical classification schemes (IPC/CPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular classification schemes are the International Patent Classification (IPC) and Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC), which are hierarchical (sections, classes, sub-classes, main groups, sub-groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification outputs often target these hierarchical codes (e.g., F02D 41/02). Evaluation and modeling may need to respect the hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject classification evaluation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Three different evaluation methods for patent classification: top prediction, top N guesses, and all categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top prediction checks whether the top-1 prediction matches the main class. Top N is successful if any of top-n predictions matches the main class (more flexible). All-categories checks whether the top-1 prediction is included among the main and incidental classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification performance metrics reported
rubrics_metrics.description: Common reported metrics include precision (P), accuracy (A), and F1 score (F1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables in the literature report precision/accuracy/F1 for models (e.g., GPT-2+CNN P=80.52, BERT P=81.75, Transformer A=56.70). Choose metric appropriate for multi-label/hierarchical setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main methodologies for patent classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Three mainstream approaches: feature extraction + classifier; fine-tuning transformer-based language models; and hybrid/multimodal methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature-extraction approaches use embeddings (bag-of-words, GloVe, Skip-gram, FastText, GPT-2) with classifiers (CNN/RNN/KNN). Transformer fine-tuning (BERT/XLNet/RoBERTa/ELECTRA, domain-adaptive pretraining, adapters) is currently mainstream. Hybrid methods combine text, image, metadata, and graph signals to improve robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset/experimental comparability and benchmark need
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers use different datasets, dataset splits, parts of patent text, and metrics, complicating comparison across methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper calls for standard benchmarks for patent classification to facilitate development and fair comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for future classification work
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus more on detailed patent descriptions (not just titles/abstracts/claims) and investigate domain-adaptive methods adapting LLMs to the patent domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions contain more specific technical information; domain adaptation can improve performance over general pre-trained embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art search (task definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a target patent document X, automatically retrieve K documents most relevant to X from a patent database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior-art search is crucial for assessing patentability; relevant results may come from distant fields with different terminology. Prior art can be non-patent literature as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent retrieval data and feature processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-processing for retrieval may use text, metadata, and images; feature transforms include TF-IDF, word/document embeddings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance ranking algorithms include BM25 (bag-of-words) and cosine similarity on vector embeddings. Choice of text representation (keyword/full-text/document-level embeddings) affects retrieval quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keyword-based vs full-text and statistical vs deep-learning tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Keyword-based methods (query expansion/reduction/hybrid) and statistical methods (e.g., BM25) are straightforward but miss semantic/contextual info. Full-text and deep-learning embeddings (Word2Vec, Doc2Vec, transformer-based embeddings) can capture more semantics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors in keyword methods arise from vocabulary mismatch and invented nomenclature in patents. Full-text/document-level embeddings have shown improvements (e.g., Doc2Vec >10% vs bag-of-words in some studies), but some transformer-based retrieval variants may not beat BM25 baselines in patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrieval evaluation metrics and baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean average precision (MAP) and other IR metrics are used to evaluate retrieval performance; BM25 is a strong baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some transformer-based methods (e.g., BERT-PLI) did not surpass BM25 baseline on patent retrieval in reported experiments; evaluate new models against established baselines like BM25 and document-level embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrieval-augmented LLMs as promising direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrating retrieval into LLMs can improve factual accuracy and downstream performance; retrieval-augmented generation is promising for patent tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior literature shows retrieval-augmented models improve QA, in-context learning, and factual grounding; applying this to patent prior-art and claim retrieval is a promising research direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent landscaping task and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent landscaping aims to retrieve patents related to a particular topic and can use keyword-based retrieval, seed-patent expansion, or classification models that decide membership in a topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscaping may be approached as topic-centered retrieval or binary classification (patent belongs to topic). Researchers have concatenated multiple embeddings (text + graph) and released labeled datasets for landscaping-oriented classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom-to-operate (FTO) search definition and core requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: FTO search (clearance search) determines if a technology/product would be covered by any active IP rights; it differs from prior-art novelty searches in that it focuses on whether an active patent's independent claim would cover (i.e., have fewer features than) the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTO requires detailed analysis of potentially relevant patent claims and breaking down the target technology into features. Automated retrieval of targeted patent claims is the core of this task; it is important but under-investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information extraction (IE) task definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Information extraction transforms textual patent data into structured formats (entities, relations, knowledge graphs) to support downstream applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IE is often a supporting task for patent analysis, recommendation, and engineering design. It can extract entities (technologies, problems, solutions), relations, and knowledge graphs for further processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: IE methodological split: rule-based vs deep-learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule-based methods use hand-crafted rules for precise and interpretable extraction; deep-learning methods (LSTM, transformers, T5, etc.) learn from labeled data and can scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule-based methods are transparent but time-consuming, brittle, and biased. Deep-learning methods require large annotated datasets and compute but handle language variability better. Example rule: 'The term user followed by can and adverbs, such as readily efficiently, quickly and easily' for affordance extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information extraction evaluation metrics and application results
rubrics_metrics.description: IE systems are evaluated with standard metrics (e.g., F1). Reported results include high F1 in targeted tasks (e.g., extracting technical problems/solutions with F1=90% in one study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance varies by task and data; deep models applied to descriptions (longer text) need architectures that handle long contexts (e.g., T5-based frameworks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal definition of novelty and features (formal patent standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is conceived as a combination of features; it is novel if there is no older document or disclosure that alone includes and/or describes all essential features of the invention. Features are outlined in the patent claims, and independent claims list the essential features. In many jurisdictions, features cannot be negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty assessment critically relies on correct identification and comparison of features. The same feature may be named differently across documents; feature variability is a major challenge for examiners and automated systems. Some offices allow negative limitations only when clearly stated in the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and inventiveness task framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty and inventiveness prediction are commonly framed as binary classification tasks (novel vs not novel), though assessing a level/degree of novelty can also be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty has a precise legal definition and is better-specified (amenable to automated approaches) than inventiveness/obviousness, which can be more ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodologies for novelty and inventiveness prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches include indicator-based methods (citation/co-classification/proximity indicators), outlier detection on embeddings (e.g., LOF on Doc2Vec/Word2Vec/LSA), and proposals to use LLMs to extract and compare explicit features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator-based methods measure technological novelty/originality (recombination, origins) but differ from formal legal novelty. Outlier detection treats novel inventions as statistical outliers; limitations include flagging unusual but not legally novel patents. The paper suggests LLMs to explicitly extract features for legally grounded novelty prediction.
